summary: Edge review of the 1.201 Indigenous person entries. Edge review of the 1.201 person entries Winona Wheeler, Brenda Macdougall, Robert Alexander Innes and Mary Jane Logan McCallum (Agent A). All 12 existing edges were checked against their sources: 9 kept, 2 revised and 1 rerouted. edge_2147 gains Wheeler's 2018 reading of Ahenakew. edge_2150 drops 'co-founder of … Shekon Neechie' for her own statements on decolonizing tribal histories. edge_2153, Innes's critique of Daschuk, moves from settler_colonialism/health_starvation to native_newcomer/reserves_schools_state: Innes frames the deaths as colonial genocide. There are 8 new edges: Wolfe → Wheeler, after her adoption of his definition with Denise Henning (2021); postcolonial studies, L. T. Smith and Deloria → Wheeler; Wheeler → indigenous (Indigenous, not ethnic, 1998) and → oral (critique); Macdougall → indigenous/peoplehood (2016); McCallum → native_newcomer (critique, via two reviewers). Also a settler_colonialism roster row for Wheeler and a revised one for McCallum, the McCallum CHR 2017 source moved to its DOI, scope notes, 12 new chronology events and a corrected PhD event. Edge review B (Simpson, Coulthard, Andersen, Trask): Coulthard dissertation locators corrected on five edges, his scope note and the dissertation's source note; edge_2164 no longer attaches Andersen's phrase about John Ralston Saul to historians; target strands set on edges 2129, 2135 and 2144; six new edges in er-B/entry-draft.json. Edge review C (2026-10-28) of LaRocque, L. T. Smith, McNickle and Life Lived Like a Story. Six new LaRocque edges from read dissertation pages: critiques of postcolonial studies, Sioui's autohistory, Mandelbaum's ethnography and fur-trade historians; Fanon and Dickason as resources. Reroutes: edge_2166's target strand to native_newcomer/historians_indian; edge_1003 now leaves from emma_larocque; edge_750 now runs from the packaged entry into ethnohistory/collaboration_authority. edge_775 reworded. Dates: When the Other Is Me corrected to 2010; McNickle's 1966 Regina post; the 1992 CHA prize on Life Lived Like a Story as the CHA lists it. The promotion01_smith citation no longer names the excluded scan host.
authorization: User, 2026-10-28: "I think this confirms Wheeler is engaged with settler colonialism studies as well?"; "we need to use research agents to review the edges more carefully"; "you should also push the indigenous update".
rationale: Research of 2026-10-28: data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-A.md. Every stage-1 item rests on a passage read, with a locator: the author's own words, or for erA_08 a named reader's explicit statement. Wheeler's texts are linked by DOI, JSTOR stable URL or the journal's site, never through self-posted copies; the dissertation carries no URL. Shekon Neechie essays are paraphrased (OCAP review #12). No Elders' words, teachings, protocol, story content or family detail are used. Abstract-only, publisher-blurb and held items are listed in stage2. Research of 2026-10-28: data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-B.md. The texts were re-read: Simpson 2007 and Trask 1991 in full, Andersen 2014 introduction pp. 3–20, and Coulthard 2009 searched in full text with the pages cited read. Every locator corrected here was checked against the page number printed on the UVic PDF. The Harris → Coulthard edge, held in 1.201 (ihB_rel_11) as a footnote citation, is included at the coordinator's direction: it rests on Coulthard's body text (p. 18, 'generally acknowledged among Canadian historians') and his conclusion (p. 215), not only on n. 48. Trask's target strand follows the coordinator's decision. Research: data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-C.md (2026-10-28). Stage 1 only: every encoded edge rests on the author's own words in pages read with locators (LaRocque 1999 dissertation), or on a named reader read in full (Black 2011; Iverson 1993; Carlson, Lutz and Schaepe 2009, read in full by Agent C on 2026-10-27). Reroutes are guarded endpoint sets; relationships are never removed. erC_07 and erC_08 and the Smith reroutes are in stage2. OCAP: no community knowledge, family detail or narrator words; the identity notes are unchanged.

edge_2147.evidence_note: Wheeler 2010, p. 49 (Cuthand 'followed the path of his mentor Edward Ahenakew'; she met Cuthand in 1982 at Manitoba), p. 53 (Ahenakew, The Plains Cree, on the Old Man as 'an institution in Indian life through the centuries') and p. 56 ('an authentic repository for the annals of his people'). Revision 1.204: in 'their brains were like paper' (Shekon Neechie, 20 June 2018; paraphrased, not reproduced), ¶¶7–12, Wheeler reads Ahenakew's Voices of the Plains Cree (Old Keyam) as a narrative strategy addressed to two audiences, with a subtext legible only to readers who share his cultural repertoire. No story content is used (OCAP).

edge_2150.relationship: Decolonizing tribal histories: the 'silencing, marginalization, and patronizing of Indigenous voices' in the writing of Indigenous histories 'epitomizes intellectual colonialism', so decolonization 'must begin from within a tribal context' (2000); Native Studies is 'a revolt against colonialist representations of Indigenous life and history' (2001); oral history belongs 'in history, as history' (2010).
edge_2150.evidence_note: Stevenson [Wheeler], Decolonizing Tribal Histories (PhD, UC Berkeley, 2000), abstract (read through OCR). Wheeler, CJNS 21:1 (2001), p. 98 (read in full). Wheeler 2010, p. 48 ('as we carve a space for Indigenous oral history in history, as history'). Revision 1.204 drops the earlier wording 'co-founder of the Indigenous-controlled Shekon Neechie': USask News (2018) records her on the site's managing board, and Innes conceived the site. The board is carried by community_engaged_indigenous/indigenous_historians_institutions.

edge_2153.evidence_note: Paraphrased (Shekon Neechie, community-controlled: cited, not reproduced). 'Clearing the Plains of Accountability' (2018), para. 2 (his aim: to hold Daschuk's argument against the scholars he cites); paras. 5–8 (Tobias 1983, Lux 2004 and Titley 1999 set against Daschuk on Dewdney); para. 14 (whether those who praised the book read the foundational literature). 'Historians and Indigenous Genocide in Saskatchewan', para. 15 (Daschuk's attempt to exonerate Dewdney contradicts previous historians). Daschuk's words are known only through Innes. Revision 1.204 reroutes the edge from settler_colonialism/health_starvation to native_newcomer/reserves_schools_state. The critique concerns Daschuk's account of Dewdney and of the state-policy historians he cites (Tobias, Lux, Titley). Innes frames the deaths as 'colonial genocide' ('Historians and Indigenous Genocide', para. 1 and n. 1), not in settler-colonial terms; 'settler' appears only in his paraphrase of Daschuk ('Clearing the Plains of Accountability', paras. 3, 11).

edge_2135.evidence_note: Own words, dissertation p. 10, and p. 37: 'Canadian settler-colonialism remains structurally oriented around achieving the same colonial effect it sought in the pre-1969 period: the dispossession of Indigenous peoples of their lands and self-determining authority'; the 2014 book p. 125 as quoted by Englert (2020, read). edge_2164.relationship: Against 'the simplistic tropes of mixedness and hybridity that seem to fascinate so many scholars who write of Métis histories': asked 'Have not fur trade historians … already extensively documented numerous instances of Métis mixedness?', he answers that to understand the Métis 'in terms of some apparently innate mixedness is thus to reproduce the same racist depictions through which less critical commentators – among them scholars – recognize indigeneity' (2014)
edge_2164.evidence_note: His own words, 'Métis': Race, Recognition, and the Struggle for Indigenous Peoplehood (UBC Press, 2014), introduction read in the publisher's sample (pp. 3–14; pp. 3–20 rechecked 2026-10-28): p. 4, 'an overly racialized narrative that connected Métis nationhood to fur trade society'; p. 5, 'the simplistic tropes of mixedness and hybridity that seem to fascinate so many scholars who write of Métis histories', in 'a vision premised on the notion that all Indigenous peoples are mixed' (he does not deny mixedness); p. 10, 'Have not fur trade historians … already extensively documented numerous instances of Métis mixedness?'; p. 11, 'To continue to understand the Métis in terms of some apparently innate mixedness is thus to reproduce the same racist depictions'; p. 12, chapter 1 treats 'a strand of long-standing fur trade literature'. In the pages read he names no fur-trade historian, so the arrow targets the frame, not Van Kirk, Brown or Peterson. Their side in their own words: Peers and Podruchny (2010, n. 2) use 'metis' for 'all descendants of European men and Aboriginal women'; Brown, as translated there (pp. 2–3, n. 3): 'there is no single Metis core identity but rather a range along a spectrum'; Brown (2017, p. 57 n. 26) names The New Peoples and Andersen's book as the older and newer poles of the field and (pp. 57–58) offers 'of mixed descent' as a descriptive term beside 'the natives’ own categories'. Chapters 1–5 unread. Person entry, identity note and the book's source record are Agent B's. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §§2.1–2.2) Revision 1.204: the phrase 'misrecognized as a hybrid off-shoot of two races' (p. 6) describes John Ralston Saul's 'métis civilization', not historians, and was removed from this edge (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-B.md).

edge_2166.evidence_note: Her own words, dissertation (1999), PDF pp. 135–136, read by Agent B (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md §1.7): Native works are 'gauged with a language of containment. Bruce Trigger's foreword to George Sioui's For An American [sic] Autohistory provides a typical example of containment'; scholars 'must make it their mandate first to comprehend the noxious nature of colonization before dismissing utterances of decolonization merely as “sloganistic,” “bitter,” “biased” or “polemical”' (p. 136). Trigger has no node; the arrow goes to the strand that holds his account of how historians wrote about Native peoples (Trigger 1986), since the passage concerns how scholars gauge Native writing, not his contact-era history (edge review C, 2026-10-28). Sioui is not the target. Requested by Agent B (ihB_rel_17).

edge_1003.evidence_note: Emma LaRocque's specified criticism in her 1999 University of Manitoba dissertation (read at PDF pp. 54 and 249); the arrow leaves from her entry since revision 1.204 (it left from the Indigenous history entry before her entry existed). She describes 'the neo cross-cultural approach adopted by Native specialist scholars from about the 1960s-1980s era (Bailey, Jaenen, Trigger, Brown, Van Kirk)', which 'tended to frame all things Native in typical terms of "cultural differences" or "traditions."' She grants: 'Compared to earlier racist material, this is, of course, a much improved approach to Native history. And with greater awareness, there is greater improvement.' But 'ethnological descriptions have a "distancing" effect', and 'This process results in Othering the very people the researcher is trying to make understandable to his or her audience' (p. 249). Her note 18 names the book: 'See in Many Tender Ties, for example, Van Kirk's listing of all the items of fashion or jewelry metis women were "very fond of" (101-103). There is an unstated assumption that such interests are abnormal or "remarkable" for these women to acquire' (p. 249, n. 18). In an earlier note she cites the book, with Saum and Ray and Freeman, among fur-trade studies that record Native resistance (PDF p. 54, note). Brown is named in the same list on p. 249 and the criticism is noted on her own entry (pe139_brown_rel_01); one arrow is drawn, to Van Kirk, because the note's example is hers. edge_868 (indigenous → native_newcomer) already carries LaRocque with Sioui and Stevenson (Wheeler) at entry level; this edge records the person-level target. OCR slips in the PDF text layer are corrected ('Van Krk', 'al1', 'hrterests'). The page numbers are PDF pages, as in edge_868. No identity classification is recorded. Later reading, labelled: Perry (2008, p. 163) dates 'sharp post-colonial, anti-racist, and post-structuralist critiques' of Van Kirk's work to the early 1990s; those texts are unread here.

edge_750.relationship: Read as ethnohistory: the Stó:lō field-school editors take Cruikshank's work with the three Yukon elders as exemplary of 'the new ethnohistorical literature' (2009), and Iverson's survey of American Indian history praises the collaboration (1993).
edge_750.evidence_note: Rerouted in revision 1.204 from oral → ethnohistory: the edge rested on this book alone, and life_lived_like_a_story → oral (edge_2174) now carries the oral-history link. Carlson, Lutz and Schaepe, 'Turning the Page' (2009), p. 2 and n. 4, read in full by Agent C on 2026-10-27 (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-community-engaged.md): 'Attention to cultural context has been a hallmark of the new ethnohistorical literature, as exemplified by Julie Cruikshank', citing the book 'in collaboration with Angela Sidney, Kitty Smith, and Annie Ned'. Iverson, introduction to the 1993 reissue of McNickle's Native American Tribalism, p. xvi (read 2026-10-28): 'Julie Cruikshank's recent collaboration with three elderly Yukon women has produced an extraordinary tapestry of Native life in Life Lived Like a Story.' Angela Sidney, Kitty Smith and Annie Ned are named contributors alongside Cruikshank; oral history is not simply raw material collected by an academic. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-C.md)

edge_775.relationship: Wrote against administrators' 'certainty that native America had vanished before the march of progress' (1973) and helped build Native history's institutions; Iverson (1993) called Native American Tribalism 'a book ahead of its time'.
edge_775.evidence_note: Historical synthesis and institution-building: the Newberry finding aid records his 1949 work and participation in creating its history centre in 1972. This is not a claim of a universal field foundation. This teaching link presents the named approach; it does not establish intellectual descent or a contribution to every part of the umbrella field. Revision 1.201 (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md): McNickle's 1973 preface (pp. xix–xx, read) challenges administrators' 'certainty that native America had vanished before the march of progress'; Iverson's 1993 introduction (p. iv, read) notes that 'few Native historians have tried to provide an overview of the national Indian experience' and (p. v) that he directed the centre in its first fellowship year, 1973–74. Edge review C (2026-10-28): Iverson, p. vi (read), the book 'was, in many ways, a book ahead of its time. Its general theme seems less innovative or path-breaking perhaps today. However, that changed perception is a commentary on how the field has been altered in ways generally presaged by this book'; Iverson also judges that McNickle's 'early analysis of the Settlement Act in Alaska now appears overly optimistic' (p. vi). (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-C.md)

source_field_sets.expect: Downloaded thesis; checked title/date and read p. 34. LaRocque relates her 1974 curriculum research to Defeathering the Indian and describes its pedagogical and resistance purposes. This is her 1999 retrospective account, not a full reading of the 1975 book or dissertation. Addendum 2026-10-14: Addendum 2026-10-14 (Claude, Van Kirk draft): reread at PDF p. 249 and n. 18 and at PDF p. 54 (OCR text layer; slips corrected). On p. 249 she describes 'the neo cross-cultural approach adopted by Native specialist scholars from about the 1960s-1980s era (Bailey, Jaenen, Trigger, Brown, Van Kirk)'. She grants that 'Compared to earlier racist material, this is, of course, a much improved approach to Native history', but writes that 'ethnological descriptions have a "distancing" effect' and that 'This process results in Othering the very people the researcher is trying to make understandable to his or her audience'. Note 18 cites Van Kirk's listing of fashion items metis women were 'very fond of' ('Many Tender Ties', pp. 101–103), with 'an unstated assumption that such interests are abnormal or "remarkable"'. The note on PDF p. 54 cites Saum, Ray and Freeman, and Van Kirk among fur-trade works that record Native resistance. Addendum 2026-10-27: Reread from the project's earlier lawful download (the repository was in maintenance): PDF pp. 8, 11, 21, 29, 37–38, 47, 70, 118–119, 135–136, 249. Walker's survey 'conservative and inadequate', 'Canadian historiography is not that benign' (p. 119); Trigger's foreword to Sioui 'a typical example of containment' (pp. 135–136); Adams's 'White Ideal' (p. 47); Said's 'pretended suprapolitical objectivity' applied to 'the Canadian academic community and its treatment of Aboriginal history' (p. 70).
